Getting Started with MultiStateTMLE

Source: vignettes/MultiStateTMLE.qmd 
library(MultiStateTMLE)

We will in this vignette use the following example: how many deaths would be prevented by a drug that makes an illness less likely?

The Data

illness_death is a simulated dataset of a trial of 200 patients who may fall ill and may die, with follow-up subject to censoring. The illness can occur at most once and raises the hazard of death. Patients were randomised to treatment (1) or placebo (0), and patients with a higher baseline biomarker are more likely to fall ill.

head(illness_death)
#>   id      time     event  biomarker treatment
#> 1  1 2.8926838 censoring  0.2724785         1
#> 2  2 0.1282264   illness  0.3572619         0
#> 3  2 1.2558891     death  0.3572619         0
#> 4  3 0.6567113     death -0.8616620         0
#> 5  4 0.1752960   illness  0.8083350         1
#> 6  4 0.2409278     death  0.8083350         1

Each row is an event: the patient id, the time of the event, which event it was, and the baseline covariates. A patient who dies without falling ill has one row, like patient 3, while one who falls ill and then dies has two, like patient 2:

illness_death[illness_death$id %in% c(2, 3), ]
#>   id      time   event  biomarker treatment
#> 2  2 0.1282264 illness  0.3572619         0
#> 3  2 1.2558891   death  0.3572619         0
#> 4  3 0.6567113   death -0.8616620         0
Simulated data

This is the format simevent::simulate_events() returns, so data simulated with simevent can be used directly. illness_death itself was simulated with simevent, which lets us check the estimates against the truth below.

Fitting the Hazards

The first step is to model the hazard of each event. fit_initial() takes one formula per event, with the event on the left and the covariates of its hazard on the right. Using another event’s name as a covariate gives its number of events so far, so death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness lets the illness change the death hazard:

models <- list(
  hazard_model(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, limit = 1),
  death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness,
  censoring ~ biomarker
)
fit <- fit_initial(illness_death, models = models, tau = 1)
fit
#> Initial fit of 200 individuals up to tau = 1
#> 
#>         name     type                                   model at_risk
#>       <char>   <char>                                  <char>  <lgcl>
#> 1:   illness one_jump         illness ~ biomarker + treatment    TRUE
#> 2:     death terminal death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness   FALSE
#> 3: censoring terminal                   censoring ~ biomarker   FALSE

By default each hazard is a Cox model, so the death hazard is

\begin{aligned} \lambda_{\text{death}}(t) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\big( & \beta_1 \, \text{biomarker} + \beta_2 \, \text{treatment} \\ & + \beta_3 \, \text{illness}(t) \big), \end{aligned}

where \text{illness}(t) is 1 once the patient has fallen ill. tau = 1 is the time horizon: everything below concerns what happens by time 1.

Hazard models

Every event in the data needs a model, censoring included. A plain formula is short for hazard_model(formula), which also takes limit, the most events a patient can have (here one illness), and at_risk, a condition such as ~ illness == 0 for when patients are at risk.

Halving the Illness

Without any intervention, tmle_estimate() estimates the risk of death by tau, given by risk():

observed <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death))
observed
#> TMLE estimate of risk(death)
#> without intervention
#> 
#>    target  estimate         se     lower     upper
#>    <char>     <num>      <num>     <num>     <num>
#> 1:  death 0.3326759 0.03439736 0.2652584 0.4000935
#> 
#> Initial estimate: 0.3327; no targeting needed, as it already solves the EIC equation

Now suppose the drug halves the hazard of the illness. scale_intensity() multiplies a hazard by a factor \alpha, and the estimate is the risk of death had the illness hazard been \alpha \lambda_{\text{illness}}(t):

halved <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death), scale_intensity(illness = 0.5))
halved
#> TMLE estimate of risk(death)
#> under scale_intensity(illness = 0.5)
#> 
#>    target  estimate         se     lower     upper
#>    <char>     <num>      <num>     <num>     <num>
#> 1:  death 0.2906665 0.03341164 0.2251809 0.3561521
#> 
#> Initial estimate: 0.2907; no targeting needed, as it already solves the EIC equation

Halving the illness lowers the risk of death from 0.333 to 0.291. The other hazards, death given illness included, are left as they are.

coef() and confint() extract the estimate and its confidence interval:

coef(halved)
#>     death 
#> 0.2906665
confint(halved, level = 0.9)
#>             5 %      95 %
#> death 0.2357092 0.3456237
Reading the output

The standard error comes from the efficient influence curve, so no bootstrap is needed. The last line gives the estimate from the initial fit alone, which TMLE then targets: it updates the fitted hazards until the estimate solves the efficient influence curve equation. This removes the first-order bias of the initial fit, so the confidence interval is valid even with flexible hazard models.

Here no targeting was needed: the Cox fits already solve the equation to within the stopping criterion, \text{se} / \log n, so the estimate is the initial estimate. With 200 patients this is common, since the remaining bias is small next to the standard error. With larger samples, or more flexible initial fits, expect one or more targeting steps.

Other interventions

A factor of 0 removes the illness, and one above 1 increases it. The factor can also be a formula in time, the baseline covariates and the events so far, for example a drug that only works early, or only for patients with biomarker > 0:

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(time < 0.5, 0.5, 1))
))
#>    death 
#> 0.302683
coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(biomarker > 0, 0.5, 1))
))
#>     death 
#> 0.3053054

Several events can be scaled at once, as in scale_intensity(illness = 0.5, death = 0.8).

From Hazards to Risks

“Halve the hazard” is hard to interpret: what does it mean for how many patients fall ill? intervention_curve() answers this for a grid of factors \alpha, estimating both the risk of the illness, the exposure, and the risk of death:

curve <- intervention_curve(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  exposure = risk(illness),
  alpha = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)
)
curve
#> Intervention curve of risk(death) against risk(illness)
#> over 6 scalings of the intensity of illness
#> 
#>    alpha target exposure_estimate exposure_se  estimate         se     lower
#>    <num> <char>             <num>       <num>     <num>      <num>     <num>
#> 1:  0.00  death         0.0000000  0.00000000 0.2336750 0.03966975 0.1559237
#> 2:  0.25  death         0.1145766  0.01453457 0.2644432 0.03553681 0.1947923
#> 3:  0.50  death         0.2169103  0.02428345 0.2906665 0.03374676 0.2245241
#> 4:  1.00  death         0.3687958  0.03488168 0.3326759 0.03427321 0.2655017
#> 5:  1.50  death         0.4790098  0.03999024 0.3645547 0.03712284 0.2917953
#> 6:  2.00  death         0.5616300  0.04251611 0.3893948 0.04055059 0.3099171
#>        upper
#>        <num>
#> 1: 0.3114263
#> 2: 0.3340941
#> 3: 0.3568089
#> 4: 0.3998502
#> 5: 0.4373141
#> 6: 0.4688724

Plotting one against the other shows how the risk of death responds to the risk of illness:

ce <- curve$estimate

plot(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$estimate,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  las = 1,
  bty = "l",
  ylim = range(ce$lower, ce$upper),
  xlab = "Risk of illness by time 1",
  ylab = "Risk of death by time 1"
)
arrows(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$lower,
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$upper,
  angle = 90,
  code = 3,
  length = 0.04
)

Removing the illness altogether (the leftmost point) lowers the risk of death by about 10 percentage points.

Checking against the truth

illness_death was simulated from the model below, so simevent can tell us the true risks under each intervention, by simulating many patients without censoring and with the illness hazard scaled by intervene:

library(simevent)

true_model <- sim_model(
  biomarker = sim_covariate(function(N) rnorm(N)),
  treatment = sim_covariate(function(N) rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)),
  illness = sim_process("transient", limit = 1, eta = 0.7, nu = 1),
  death = sim_process("terminal", eta = 0.3, nu = 1),
  censoring = sim_process("censoring", eta = 0.1, nu = 1),
  effects = list(
    sim_effect(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, coef = c(0.5, -1)),
    sim_effect(death ~ illness + treatment, coef = c(1.2, -0.3))
  )
)

true_risks <- function(intervene) {
  sim <- simulate_events(
    true_model,
    n = 1e5,
    cens = 0,
    intervene = intervene,
    seed = 1
  )
  risks <- event_risk(sim, true_model, c("illness", "death"), tau = 1)
  setNames(risks$risk, risks$process)
}

check <- ce[, c("alpha", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- sapply(
  check$alpha,
  function(alpha) true_risks(list(illness = alpha))["death"]
)
check
#>    alpha  estimate     lower     upper   truth
#>    <num>     <num>     <num>     <num>   <num>
#> 1:  0.00 0.2336750 0.1559237 0.3114263 0.22972
#> 2:  0.25 0.2644432 0.1947923 0.3340941 0.25350
#> 3:  0.50 0.2906665 0.2245241 0.3568089 0.27619
#> 4:  1.00 0.3326759 0.2655017 0.3998502 0.31160
#> 5:  1.50 0.3645547 0.2917953 0.4373141 0.34098
#> 6:  2.00 0.3893948 0.3099171 0.4688724 0.36302

Every interval covers the truth, and the estimates follow the true curve closely, removing the illness included.

Calibrating the Drug

Often the question is about risks directly: what if the drug prevented 20% of illnesses? calibrate() finds the factor \alpha for which the risk of illness reaches a given value, and estimates the risk of death under it:

calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
)
calibrated
#> TMLE estimate of risk(death)
#> under calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
#> 
#>    quantity  estimate         se     lower     upper
#>      <char>     <num>      <num>     <num>     <num>
#> 1:    alpha 0.7443751 0.01232345 0.7202216 0.7685287
#> 2:    theta 0.2950367 0.02790535 0.2403432 0.3497301
#> 
#> Estimates under the calibrated intervention:
#>    target  estimate         se    lower     upper   se_crude
#>    <char>     <num>      <num>    <num>     <num>      <num>
#> 1:  death 0.3127176 0.03330144 0.247448 0.3779872 0.03338458

The first table gives the calibrated \alpha and the risk of illness \theta it reaches, 80% of the observed 0.369. The second gives the risk of death under it.

Calibration rules

The target risk of illness can be given in three ways:

  • level(theta): the risk is theta.
  • absolute_change(delta): the risk is delta plus its observed value.
  • relative_change(rho): the risk is rho times its observed value.

Because \alpha is itself estimated, the standard error se accounts for its uncertainty. se_crude is the standard error if \alpha were known.

years_lost() gives the expected years of life lost before tau instead of the risk, and can be used wherever risk() can:

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  years_lost(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
))
#>     death 
#> 0.1596098

Explaining a Treatment Effect

So far treatment has only been a covariate. Suppose instead we want its effect on death, and how much of it is because treated patients fall ill less often. The calibrated intervention above answers this: give patients the treatment, but calibrate their risk of illness to what it would have been on placebo. This splits the total effect into two contrasts:

  • mediated: treatment versus the calibrated intervention, the part that goes through the illness, and
  • calibrated: the calibrated intervention versus placebo, the rest.

treatment_model tells fit_initial() how treatment was assigned, so that estimates can be made with everyone treated or everyone on placebo:

trial_fit <- fit_initial(
  illness_death,
  models = models,
  tau = 1,
  treatment_model = treatment ~ biomarker
)

a sets everyone’s treatment, and reference_a = 0 calibrates the risk of illness to that under placebo:

treated <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 1)
placebo <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 0)
treated_calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  trial_fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(1), reference_a = 0),
  a = 1
)
treated_calibrated
#> TMLE estimate of risk(death)
#> under calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(1), reference_a = 0), with a = 1
#> 
#>    quantity  estimate         se     lower    upper
#>      <char>     <num>      <num>     <num>    <num>
#> 1:    alpha 2.6814303 0.72116544 1.2679720 4.094889
#> 2:    theta 0.4974118 0.05135867 0.3967507 0.598073
#> 
#> Estimates under the calibrated intervention:
#>    target  estimate         se    lower     upper   se_crude
#>    <char>     <num>      <num>    <num>     <num>      <num>
#> 1:  death 0.3112979 0.06357508 0.186693 0.4359028 0.06411261

To give treated patients the risk of illness they would have had on placebo, their illness hazard must be multiplied by about 2.7. calibrated_contrasts() then combines the three fits:

contrasts <- calibrated_contrasts(treated, placebo, treated_calibrated)
contrasts
#> Decomposition of the effect of a on death into mediated and calibrated contrasts
#> 
#>    target   contrast    estimate         se      lower         upper
#>    <char>     <char>       <num>      <num>      <num>         <num>
#> 1:  death      total -0.18273318 0.06913193 -0.3182293 -0.0472370913
#> 2:  death   mediated -0.06387838 0.03275458 -0.1280762  0.0003194037
#> 3:  death calibrated -0.11885480 0.08063644 -0.2768993  0.0391897229

Treatment lowers the risk of death by 18 percentage points, of which 6 go through the illness.

Checking against the truth

With true_model from before, simevent gives the true contrasts too: simulate each arm without censoring, and for the calibrated arm search for the factor on the illness hazard that matches the risk of illness on placebo:

placebo_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 0))
treatment_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1))
true_alpha <- uniroot(
  function(alpha) {
    calibrated <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = alpha))
    calibrated["illness"] - placebo_risks["illness"]
  },
  interval = c(1, 5),
  tol = 0.01
)$root
calibrated_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = true_alpha))

check <- contrasts$estimate[, c("contrast", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- c(
  treatment_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"],
  treatment_risks["death"] - calibrated_risks["death"],
  calibrated_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"]
)
check
#>      contrast    estimate      lower         upper    truth
#>        <char>       <num>      <num>         <num>    <num>
#> 1:      total -0.18273318 -0.3182293 -0.0472370913 -0.13528
#> 2:   mediated -0.06387838 -0.1280762  0.0003194037 -0.05329
#> 3: calibrated -0.11885480 -0.2768993  0.0391897229 -0.08199

Every interval covers the truth. With 200 patients the contrasts are estimated less precisely than the risks, since each compares two arms of about 100.

Where Next

  • risk() and years_lost() take several events at once, as in risk(death, illness), count only events in some states, as in risk(death, when = ~ illness == 0), and for recurrent events give the expected number of events, or the risk of a first one with only_first = TRUE. See ?"target-parameters".
  • To simulate event history data, and the truth under interventions, see simevent.
